books.section: Gender, Voluntary Organizations, and Social Reform

primary_sources: Carry A. Nation, The Use and Need of the Life of Carry A. Nation (1905)

stimulus.text:
“I never told anyone then of my intention of smashing saloons in Wichita. I took a valise with me, and in that valise I put a rod of iron, perhaps a foot long, and as large around as my thumb. I also took a cane with me. I found out by smashing in Kiowa that I could use a rock but once, so I took the cane with me. I got down to Wichita about seven o’clock in the evening, that day, and went to the hotel near the Santa Fe depot and left my valise. . . . The police standing with the others. This outrage of law and decency was in violation of the oaths taken by every city officer, including mayor and councilmen, and they were as much bound to destroy these joints as they would be to arrest a murderer, or break up a den of thieves, but many of these so-called officers encouraged the violation of the law and patronized these places. I have often explained that this was the scheme of politicians and brewers to make prohibition a failure, by encouraging in every way the violation of the constitution.”

(Carry A. Nation, The Use and Need of the Life of Carry A. Nation, 1905, describing her Wichita raid of December 1900)
stimulus.source_note: Carry A. Nation, The Use and Need of the Life of Carry A. Nation (1905). Public domain; wording checked against the Project Gutenberg text (ebook 1485) as reproduced by BookRags. The book was published in 1905 and describes the Wichita raid of December 1900; Kansas had written prohibition into its constitution in 1880.

stem: What does Nation’s account show about Kansas prohibition in 1900?

options.text: Kansas had no law against selling liquor at all
options.misconception: Nation says saloons violated the constitution, so a prohibition law existed.

options.text: City officers closed every saloon as soon as it opened its doors
options.misconception: The officers encouraged the violations and patronized the saloons.

options.text: The law existed but officials refused to enforce it, so reformers acted directly
The brewers supported prohibition and willingly obeyed the law
options.misconception: Nation says brewers schemed to make prohibition fail by encouraging violations.

rationales.A: A constitution was being violated, so prohibition was the law in Kansas.
rationales.B: Officers stood with the drinkers and encouraged the lawbreaking, not the closing.
rationales.C: The law was on the books, officers would not enforce it, and Nation smashed saloons herself.
rationales.D: Brewers are named as schemers against prohibition, not as its supporters.
rationales.general:
Put Nation’s two complaints together.
1. Saloons sold drink openly, in violation of the constitution.
2. City officers were bound by oath to destroy these joints.
3. Instead the officers encouraged the violations and patronized the saloons.
4. A law unenforced leaves reformers to act on their own, which is what Nation did.
Remember: a law nobody enforces is a reformer’s reason to act alone.
